newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: Argentine relatives want dead to stay on Falklands.
newsitem.headline: Argentine relatives want dead to stay on Falklands.

text.p: Relatives of Argentine troops who died trying to capture the Falklands say their next-of-kin should remain buried on the disputed archipelago despite objections from the pro-British islanders.

"My brother's blood was spilled on these islands and he died for his country, therefore he should remain in the Malvinas," said Alejandro Arrigoni, a student from Buenos Aires whose brother Miguel Angel Falcon died in the 1982 war.
Arrigoni was in a group of 15 relatives who visited the Argentine war cemetery near Darwin on a two-day trip to the south Atlantic islands that was due to end on Thursday.
Despite official rapprochement between Britain and Argentina, the Falklanders remain deeply mistrustful of a country that still lays claim to the islands, known in Buenos Aires as the Malvinas.
Falklands councillors have called on the Argentine government to exhume its war dead, so far without success, fearing visits by mourning relatives.

British authorities have urged the Falklanders to take a more conciliatory approach in line with a detente that brought renewed diplomatic ties in 1989, high-profile visits to Argentina by British royals and rapid expansion of trade links.
This week's trip -- another group of 15 will visit in February -- follows similar such visits in 1986, 1991 and 1995.
The repeated visits have angered Falklands councillors, who wanted a larger, one-off visit. They were also opposed to the families staying overnight and being lodged at Darwin.
"We have had to concede on all three of our demands," said councillor Norma Edwards. Councillors said they had done so on humanitarian grounds.

Yet hardliners in Buenos Aires rule out repatriation, saying the bodies are already buried on Argentine soil. "One cannot repatriate within your own country," said Hector Cisneros, president of the Argentine Dependent Families Association.
The Darwin cemetery contains 234 bodies of which only 111 are identified. The rest of Argentina's war dead were lost at sea.
Hoping the graves of their loved ones were among those with names, the relatives held an emotional late-evening mass on Wednesday at the neat cemetery.

"I've waited 15 years to find the truth and now my emotions have been stirred by this journey. It's my first opportunity to visit the islands and I will cherish it," said Beatriz Rosario Salguero, whose 33-year-old husband was killed in action.

The group of mourners, chilled by a stiff evening wind, spread across the graveyard hoping to find a small wooden cross bearing the name of their loved one. Some were disappointed. Others found what they came for and wept uncontrollably.

Strangers before they left Buenos Aires on Wednesday, the mourners -- five mothers, two fathers, one widow and seven siblings of dead servicemen -- huddled around Priest Guillermo Constantini for a mass as the sun sunk over the islands.
A single carnation was placed on each grave, some marked with the inscription: "An Argentine soldier known unto God".
